stories.title: Micronesia: island chains and connections
stories.subtitle: Occupation, worked landscapes, exchange and colonial encounters
stories.description: Compare Palau, Yap, the Caroline and Marshall atolls and existing monumental-site histories without treating Micronesia as a single culture.

scenes.title: Early places have distinct histories
scenes.body: Compare Ulong’s occupation evidence with the cemetery at Chelechol ra Orrak and the atlas’s separate Bapot chronology in the Marianas. These are different sites and activities within a region whose settlement cannot be reduced to one departure, people or date. Archaeological and linguistic evidence need to be compared at the appropriate scale.
scenes.note: Rounded Palau ages and the separate revised Bapot range are retained.

scenes.title: Atoll formation is older than settlement evidence
scenes.body: At Utrōk and Maloelap, researchers dated sediments that built the islands and charcoal from cultural layers. The oldest cultural dates follow islet formation by centuries. These separate clocks prevent a landscape age being mistaken for a human arrival. Farther south, Ebon’s sampled mollusc record reveals long-term harvesting adapted to local habitats, reminding us that food and environmental knowledge belong at the centre of atoll history.
scenes.note: The two oldest cultural dates are about 1850 and 1790 cal BP. Ebon’s broad foraging study remains undated in the atlas.

scenes.title: People reshape islands
scenes.body: Babeldaob’s earthworks created substantial working and living landscapes. Ulong’s plant and sediment evidence records another way of studying human activity. Terraces, gardens and coastal settlements do not all preserve the same things: visible monumentality and subtle environmental traces can reveal complementary histories of labor and food.
scenes.note: Regional phase windows are not dates for every structure or field.

scenes.title: Atolls participate in wider exchange
scenes.body: Pottery attributed to Palau in a dated Ngulu midden demonstrates movement between different island environments. Finds at Lamotrek extend the geographic questions farther east, although their inspected source lacks a usable date. Material provenance establishes movement; it does not recover the number of exchanges, the crews or every intervening island.
scenes.note: Ngulu AD 800–1400 context; Lamotrek remains unplaced.

scenes.title: Different monumental island worlds
scenes.body: Nan Madol, Leluh and Palau’s stonework villages show communities building in different materials and settings. The atlas already records separate construction contexts at Nan Madol and a sea-level-related Leluh estimate. Their histories should stay separate while comparison opens questions about labor, water, food and political authority.
scenes.note: The scene uses existing records rather than duplicating their dates or inventing one island-chain phase.

scenes.title: A workforce travels to its material
scenes.body: At Metuker, Yapese quarrying involved foreign access rights, skilled manufacture and ways of moving stone across difficult ground. Other named Palauan quarries show coastal and inland settings. This network is distinctive because workers traveled to obtain and shape a valued material and then arranged its return by sea.
scenes.note: 1750 is within the explicitly approximate onset interpretation; other quarry dates remain unresolved.

scenes.title: Encounters could be accidental or planned
scenes.body: Antelope’s wreck near Ulong created a prolonged encounter in 1783. A Lamotrek voyage to Guam in 1787 deliberately sought iron. The contrast matters: islanders were neither isolated until a ship found them nor passive recipients of every new object. Particular journeys involved distinct purposes, relationships and consequences.
scenes.note: The two events have separate years; the line is only the Lamotrek–Guam connection.

scenes.title: Named ships join older connections
scenes.body: Vesta’s returning quarry workers and Swan’s reported cargo of stones show changing transport opportunities. Taraang’s trading operation connected copra, shipping and households to wider markets. These are specific historical links, not a complete list of traffic, and they did not replace the social histories through which objects acquired value.
scenes.note: Voyage dates and the Taraang tenure window stay distinct.

scenes.title: New administrations and new communications
scenes.body: Spanish administrators established themselves on Yap in 1886. International cables later connected the island with distant ports, and Japanese seizure followed in 1914. These changes joined military, commercial and communication networks to inhabited islands. The map marks events and infrastructure without implying that outside flags describe all local power or everyday life.
scenes.note: No automatic extension beyond 1934; later mandates and warfare require separate evidence.
